**Teams:** one or two students per machine. Pairs: one of you *drives* (keyboard), the other *navigates* (owns the sheet, calls the predictions). **Swap roles at the half-time whistle.** Both of you must be able to explain every command afterwards.

## What you'll be able to do after this lab

| | |
|---|---|
| **Identity & orientation** | `pwd`, `whoami`, `hostname`, `uname`, `history`, `clear` |
| **Files & navigation** | `ls` (`-l -a -R`), `cd`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm -i`, `cat`, `less`, `nano` |
| **Getting code** | `tar`, `wget` |
| **Toolchain & composition** | `gcc`, `./prog`, `>` , `|`, `wc`, `man`, `--help`, tab-completion |
| **Permissions** | reading `rwx`, `chmod +x`, octal `755` (yes — that's *binary*, from this week's lecture) |
| **Processes** | `Ctrl-C`, `&`, `ps`, `kill` — the fire extinguisher |
| **System info** | `df -h`, `du -sh`, `env`, `echo $PATH` |

## Pre-lab (at home, ~30 min, strongly recommended)

Play the first four modules of [Linux Survival](https://linuxsurvival.com/welcome/) — a *simulated* terminal, impossible to break. If you want a real one in your browser: [Webminal](https://www.webminal.org/).

## One idea before you type anything

The terminal is the course's third machine. It has a vocabulary of words; it runs the ritual you have already watched twice — **read a command → execute it → print → repeat** — and it does *exactly what you say, never what you mean*. Everything you learned from the Turtle applies. Everything.

## Act 0 · Install (10 min)

The lab pack is pre-placed on each machine (ask where). If it isn't — or you're at home — fetch it from the course site:

```
wget https://acads-iit-jammu.github.io/csp-f26-dhavala/labs/lab01.tar.gz
```

Then:

```
tar xzf lab01.tar.gz
cd lab01
./install.sh
```

The installer will *tell you* which branch it thinks you are (it reads the machine's name and today's date — ask yourself: how?), ask for your team's roll number(s), and build your session workspace: `/home/student/csp_labs_f26/w02-l01-<branch>-sd`. (Practising at home, where that path doesn't exist? The installer switches to *practice mode* and creates the workspace right where you ran it — everything else works identically.) **This machine is shared and forgets everything** — your workspace lives for today only; your work leaves with you at the end (Act 5).

Now the most important command of the day. Go to your workspace and start the recorder:

```
cd /home/student/csp_labs_f26/w02-l01-*-sd
script session.txt
```

Everything you type and see is now being recorded — your lab's own machine diary. (To stop it later: `exit`.)

## Act 1 · Claim the machine (10 min)

Who are you, where are you, on what? Run each, **predict its output first** where you can, then capture the passport:

```
whoami          # surprise: you are ALL 'student'. Remember this for Act 5.
hostname
uname -a
df -h .
```

Now make the machine's passport — your first *redirection* (`>` sends output into a file instead of the screen):

```
whoami > passport.txt
hostname >> passport.txt
uname -a >> passport.txt
df -h . >> passport.txt
cat passport.txt
```

## Act 2 · Build the home (25 min)

Missions, each a mini spec-card: the **ENSURES** tells you what must be true when you're done — *you* build it. Before every `ls`, say out loud what it will print — *then* press Enter.

1. **Create a `notes/` directory — your lab notebook.** Two files will live in it: `README.txt` (one line saying what lives where in this workspace) and `answers.txt`, where you'll write your answers to the **think-questions** this sheet asks along the way (they're marked ✍️). Your notebook travels home in your bundle — we read it.
   **ENSURES:** `cat notes/README.txt` prints your line. (Tools: `mkdir`, `nano`.)
2. **Build a `practice/` tree, from nothing, yourself** — you are the one creating every directory and file here. Target shape:
   ```
   practice/
   ├── a/one.txt
   ├── a/two.txt
   └── b/one.txt
   ```
   Rules of the game: make the directories (`mkdir -p practice/a practice/b`), create the *first* file empty (`touch`), but the other two files may **not** be created by `touch` — one must be born as a **copy** (`cp`) and one must *arrive* by being **moved** (`mv`) from somewhere else you made. (So you'll create a scratch file and move it — that's the point.)
   **ENSURES:** `ls -R practice` matches the diagram exactly. Predict the output on paper first.
3. Now **remove your `practice/` tree** — your first `rm`. Do it the careful way: `rm -ri practice` and read every question it asks before answering. `rm` has no undo, no bin, no mercy. Respect it today, every day.
   **ENSURES:** `ls` no longer shows `practice`. (`notes/` stays — it's real; `practice/` was scaffolding.)
4. **Rescue skills** — get stuck on purpose: open `man ls`, find what `-a` does, quit (`q`). Try `ls --help`. Press Tab twice after typing `pass`. These three moves answer 90% of the questions you'd otherwise ask us.

## Act 3 · Make it speak (20 min)

Your starter files are already in the workspace (the installer fetched them — at home you'd `wget` them from the course site).

```
nano hello.c        # change CHANGE_ME to your name (both of you, for pairs)
gcc hello.c -o hello
./hello
./hello > output.txt
cat output.txt | wc -w
```

You just compiled a real C program — the same `printf` whose descent you watched, floor by floor, in Week 1. You'll understand every line by Week 4; today it's the telescope check. ✍️ *Think-question 1, into `notes/answers.txt`:* why the `./`? Run `echo $PATH` and reason it out — ask us at the end if it doesn't click.

## Act 4 · Kill the runaway (15 min)

Week 2's Toy Computer trapped itself in an infinite ping-pong and could only be Reset. Real machines give you a fire extinguisher. The starter `loop.c` is a program that *never stops on purpose*:

```
gcc loop.c -o loop
./loop                 # watch it run away... then Ctrl-C  (extinguisher #1)
./loop &               # now it runs in the BACKGROUND — no Ctrl-C can reach it
ps                     # find its PID (the process's roll number)
kill <PID>             # extinguisher #2
ps                     # verify the fire is out
```

Every programmer writes an infinite loop eventually. Now you've already survived one.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Note the PID you just killed — and remember this:** these three commands (`./loop &`, `ps`, `kill <PID>`) are **one-time** commands. They must **NOT** go into your `replay.sh` in Act 5. That PID number was true for one moment on one machine; replayed later it could kill someone else's process.
:::

## Act 5 · Lock up, leave a diary, take your work (20 min)

1. Look at a permission string: `ls -l hello`. Decode `rwxr-xr-x` on paper: three groups of three bits — `111 101 101` = octal `755`. **This week's number systems, wearing work clothes.**
2. Try `chmod 600 passport.txt`, then `ls -l passport.txt`. ✍️ *Think-question 2, into `notes/answers.txt`:* you are *all* logged in as `student` — so who exactly did you just lock out? (Honest answer: nobody in this room. `chmod` guards between *users*, and this whole room is one user. That is what permissions really are — and why real systems give each person their own account.)
3. Your recorded history is a *log*. Now turn it into a *program*:
   ```
   history > replay.sh
   nano replay.sh        # edit! — rules below
   ```
   ::: {.callout-important}
   **Editing rules — read before touching `replay.sh`:**

   1. Every line starts with a **number** (`  501  ./hello`). Those are history bookkeeping, **not commands** — a replay would try to run a program called `501`. **Delete every line number.**
   2. Make the very first line exactly: `#!/bin/sh` — it tells the machine which language this program speaks.
   3. **KEEP** only commands that make sense *every* time they run: `./hello`, `cat output.txt | wc -w`, `ls -l`.
   4. **DELETE** `./loop &` — a replay would start a runaway with nobody watching.
   5. **DELETE** `ps` and `kill <PID>` — that PID was true for one moment of one afternoon. Replay it tomorrow on this shared machine and you might kill a stranger's process.
   6. The self-check **runs your replay.sh** and fails it if any of this is still wrong. That is deliberate.
   :::

   Now run it — **before** doing anything else:
   ```
   ./replay.sh
   ```
   `Permission denied`! **This is not an error — it is a lesson.** A freshly created file is not allowed to run; you must grant it the execute permission yourself:
   ```
   chmod +x replay.sh
   ./replay.sh
   ```

   ✍️ *Bonus for `notes/answers.txt`:* in one line, what is the difference between a log and a program? (Hint: a log records what *happened*; a program must be true *whenever* it runs.) Anything you can do, you can automate — but only the repeatable parts.
4. Stop the recorder (`exit` — you'll see "Script done"), then run the self-check and make it all green:
   ```
   ./check.sh
   ```
   Red lines tell you *what's* missing, never *how* — that's your job. When green (or when time is up — an imperfect bundle beats no bundle; the verdicts travel with it):
   ```
   ./check.sh --bundle
   ```
5. The bundle (`../lab01_<rolls>_<branch>_w02.tar.gz`) **is your work**. Copy it out — Moodle upload (link announced in lab), and *always* also email yourself a copy. Then leave the machine clean: your workspace will be swept automatically before the next lab.
